usage.goal: Learn to count and confirm small quantities in everyday adult tasks.
usage.canDoStatement: Can understand and use numbers from one to fifteen to count familiar people and objects.

scenes.scenario: At a small office, one folder is on the first tray, two folders are on the second, and three folders are on the third. The tray beside the clipboard has three folders.

check.question: According to the situation, which option gives the correct number or quantity?

scenes.imageBrief: Office desk with three clearly separated trays holding exactly 1, 2, and 3 identical folders. Put the 3-folder tray beside a clipboard and make it the focal tray. Every folder must be individually countable; no written numbers, labels, logos or watermarks.
scenes.imageAlt: Three office trays hold one, two and three folders; the three-folder tray is beside a clipboard.

scenes.scenario: At a café counter, four cups are on one tray, five on another, and six on a third. The tray nearest the kettle holds five cups.

check.question: How many cups are on the tray nearest the kettle?

scenes.imageBrief: Café counter with three separated trays holding exactly 4, 5, and 6 identical cups. Place the 5-cup tray nearest a kettle. Keep all cups easy to count; no labels or logos.
scenes.imageAlt: Three trays hold four, five and six cups; the five-cup tray is nearest a kettle.

scenes.scenario: A storeroom has three neat groups of boxes: seven, eight, and nine. The group beside the open door contains nine boxes.

check.question: Which quantity matches the selected group?

scenes.imageBrief: Storeroom with three separated groups of identical boxes: exactly 7, 8, and 9. Put the 9-box group beside an open door and make it easy to distinguish.
scenes.imageAlt: Three groups contain seven, eight and nine boxes; nine boxes are beside the open door.

scenes.scenario: At a reception desk, three ticket stacks contain ten, eleven, and twelve tickets. The middle stack contains eleven tickets.

check.question: How many tickets are in the middle stack?

scenes.imageBrief: Reception desk with three tidy ticket stacks representing 10, 11, and 12. Make the 11-ticket stack clearly central; use countable tickets with no printed text.
scenes.imageAlt: Three ticket stacks show ten, eleven and twelve tickets; eleven are in the middle.

scenes.scenario: A course coordinator prepares three sets of notebooks: thirteen, fourteen, and fifteen. The set on the right contains fifteen notebooks.

check.question: How many notebooks are in the set on the right?

scenes.imageBrief: Adult training-room supply table with three neat notebook sets of exactly 13, 14, and 15. Make the 15-notebook set clearly on the right; no written labels.
scenes.imageAlt: Three notebook sets show thirteen, fourteen and fifteen; fifteen are on the right.

reading.title: Checking the Meeting Supplies
reading.text: Maya is preparing a small meeting room before colleagues arrive. She counts six chairs, eight water bottles, and ten printed agendas, then checks whether the numbers match the booking. A coworker brings three more cups and one spare notebook. Together they recount the supplies and confirm that the room is ready without using complicated calculations.
reading.imageBrief: Friendly classroom scene matching the story with a teacher, students, windows, tables, bags, books, and wall pictures.

video.title: Count With Me
video.idea: 30–45 second video. A learner looks around a room and counts objects aloud, then pauses to let the viewer answer before revealing the number.
video.scriptStarter: I see one clock. There are two windows. I see three plants. How many chairs can you see?

usage.goal: Learn to understand and state larger numbers used in prices, rooms, queues, and totals.
usage.canDoStatement: Can recognize and say common numbers from sixteen to one million in familiar practical contexts.

scenes.scenario: A queue display shows the numbers 16, 17, and 18. The highlighted ticket number is 18.
scenes.imageBrief: Clean service-counter queue display showing only the numerals 16, 17, and 18. Highlight 18 with a simple border or light. Numerals are essential educational content; no other text or logos.
scenes.imageAlt: A queue display shows 16, 17 and 18, with 18 highlighted.

scenes.scenario: A booking screen shows room numbers 19, 20, and 30. Room 20 is highlighted.

check.question: According to the situation, which option gives the correct number or quantity?

scenes.imageBrief: Simple hotel booking screen showing only 19, 20, and 30 as large room numbers. Highlight 20; no other words, logos or interface clutter.
scenes.imageAlt: Room numbers 19, 20 and 30 appear, with 20 highlighted.

scenes.scenario: A digital counter compares 40, 50, and 60. The centre display shows 60.

check.question: Which number appears on the centre display?

scenes.imageBrief: Three clean digital displays showing 40, 50, and 60. Make 60 the central highlighted display; no other text.
scenes.imageAlt: Digital displays show 40, 50 and 60, with 60 in the centre.

scenes.scenario: A timetable screen shows the numbers 70, 80, and 90. The highlighted number is 80.

check.question: According to the situation, which option gives the correct number or quantity?

scenes.imageBrief: Simple timetable-style screen with large numerals 70, 80, and 90 only. Highlight 80; no other text, labels or logos.
scenes.imageAlt: A screen shows 70, 80 and 90, with 80 highlighted.

scenes.scenario: At a booking screen, a digital display compares hundred, thousand, and million. The highlighted figure represents million.

check.question: Which word describes the highlighted figure?

scenes.imageBrief: Adult booking screen with a clean digital display showing the quantities hundred, thousand, and million as numerals. Highlight Million; no unrelated text or branding.
scenes.imageAlt: Booking screen scene illustrating hundred, thousand, and million, with Million highlighted.

reading.title: Numbers at the Service Desk
reading.text: A hotel worker checks a booking screen before a busy weekend. Room requests include sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, and twenty guests. Larger group bookings show thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, and ninety people. The conference summary shows one hundred places. One report records one thousand bookings, while the company website records one million visits across all its locations.

usage.goal: Learn to use ordinal numbers and basic calculation words in simple practical tasks.
usage.canDoStatement: Can understand basic position words and simple arithmetic language in familiar situations.

scenes.scenario: Three adults wait in a queue. One person is first, one is second, and one is third. The person holding a blue folder is second.

check.question: Where is the marked person or item in the order?

scenes.imageBrief: Side view of an adult queue with exactly three people in first, second and third positions. The second person holds a blue folder. No written ordinal labels.
scenes.imageAlt: Three adults stand in a queue; the second person holds a blue folder.

scenes.scenario: A lift stops on the fourth, fifth, and sixth floors. The highlighted stop is the fifth floor.

check.question: Which ordinal word matches the selected position?

scenes.imageBrief: Simple lift/elevator indicator with essential numerals 4, 5, and 6, highlighting floor 5. No other written text or branding.
scenes.imageAlt: A lift indicator shows floors four, five and six, with the fifth highlighted.

scenes.scenario: A race result board shows seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth places. The highlighted runner finished tenth.

check.question: Which place in the sequence is being shown?

scenes.imageBrief: Adult fun-run finish area with four result positions represented clearly as 7th, 8th, 9th and 10th; highlight the runner in 10th. Essential ordinal numerals only.
scenes.imageAlt: A race result shows seventh through tenth place, with tenth highlighted.

scenes.scenario: On a booking screen, a simple calculation demonstrates addition and equals. The highlighted operation or result is equals.

check.question: What operation does the example in the booking screen show?

scenes.imageBrief: Adult training-style visual at a booking screen showing separate, simple calculation examples for addition and equals. Highlight Equals; use only essential mathematical symbols.
scenes.imageAlt: Booking screen scene illustrating addition and equals, with Equals highlighted.

scenes.scenario: During an invoice review, a simple calculation demonstrates subtraction, multiplication, and division. The highlighted operation or result is division.

check.question: Which calculation term is being used in the invoice?

scenes.imageBrief: Adult training-style visual at a invoice review showing separate, simple calculation examples for subtraction, multiplication, and division. Highlight Division; use only essential mathematical symbols.
scenes.imageAlt: Invoice review scene illustrating subtraction, multiplication, and division, with Division highlighted.

reading.title: Reading a Simple Score Sheet
reading.text: A training coordinator checks a short score sheet after a workshop. One team is first, another is second, and a third team is third. The coordinator also reviews a simple total using addition and subtraction, then checks whether the final figures equal the expected result. Multiplication and division appear only in a few basic examples on the sheet.
reading.imageBrief: Split scene: first panel shows the race winners; second panel shows a class number game on a board.

video.scriptStarter: Lina is first. Omar is second. Adam is third. Now let’s play: two plus three equals five.

usage.goal: Learn to understand common calculation symbols and percentage language in everyday transactions.
usage.canDoStatement: Can follow very simple calculations using plus, minus, times, divided by, and percentage.

scenes.scenario: A simple calculation card compares plus, minus, and times. The highlighted example removes two objects from a group, so it represents minus.

check.question: Which calculation term is being used in the scene?

scenes.imageBrief: Three clean visual calculation examples using objects: combining for plus, removing for minus, equal repeated groups for times. Highlight the minus example. Symbols may appear, but no explanatory text.
scenes.imageAlt: Three arithmetic examples with the subtraction/minus example highlighted.

scenes.scenario: At a reception desk, a simple calculation demonstrates divided by and percentage. The highlighted operation or result is percentage.

check.question: Which maths word matches the selected calculation?

scenes.imageBrief: Adult training-style visual at a reception desk showing separate, simple calculation examples for divided by and percentage. Highlight Percentage; use only essential mathematical symbols.
scenes.imageAlt: Reception desk scene illustrating divided by and percentage, with Percentage highlighted.

reading.title: Checking the Bill
reading.text: At a café, Karim checks the bill before paying. The cashier explains that one item is added with plus, a discount is shown with minus, and a percentage applies to the final amount. Karim asks how the total was calculated. The cashier shows the simple steps, including times and divided by, so he can confirm the amount.
reading.imageBrief: Simple classroom math lesson with a board and a percentage pie chart.

video.title: Math Symbols Around Us
video.idea: 30–40 second video. The teacher points to symbols and students answer simple problems aloud.
video.scriptStarter: This is plus. This is minus. Six divided by two is three. Fifty percent means half.
